props.title: Cat Soup
props.initialSlug: A surreal journey to save a sister's lost soul

sections.content: Cat Soup stands as one of experimental animation's most surreal masterpieces, following directly in the footsteps of Mind Game (2004) and Angel's Egg (1985). Director Tatsuo Sato crafts a 32-minute fever dream about a cat trying to save his sister's soul, channeling the manga work of Nekojiru with haunting, psychedelic imagery. Like Belladonna of Sadness (1973), it pushes animation into abstract, often disturbing territory while maintaining a hypnotic beauty.

sections.content: The film's dreamlike narrative draws from the same well as Paprika (2006) and Perfect Blue (1997), where reality bends and transforms without warning. But while those films maintain some narrative throughline, Cat Soup deliberately fractures conventional storytelling. Its closest spiritual companion might be Fantastic Planet (1973), sharing its alien landscapes and philosophical undertones about existence itself.

The animation technique merges traditional hand-drawn work with early digital effects, creating a unique aesthetic that influenced later experimental works like The Night is Short, Walk on Girl (2017) and Tekkonkinkreet (2006). The film's use of color and space, particularly in its apocalyptic sequences, echoes through modern surrealist animation like Dead Leaves (2004). SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Animation

sections.content: Cat Soup's influence extends beyond anime into global animation. Its DNA can be found in western experimental works like It's Such a Beautiful Day (2012) and World of Tomorrow (2015). The film's fearless approach to mixing cute character designs with disturbing imagery paved the way for shows like Adventure Time (2010-2018) and The Midnight Gospel (2020).
